opus-5.5.text:
I think competition is one of the central reasons the "just turn it off" story is less reassuring than it sounds. In the abstract, if an AI system starts doing something bad, you'd pull the plug. But that assumes there's a single actor who can make that decision and who bears no real cost from making it.

In practice, once AI systems are doing a large share of the economically and militarily important work, shutting them down is a sacrifice. If you're a company and your competitor keeps running their systems while you turn yours off, you lose market share, maybe you go out of business. If you're a country and your rival keeps their AI-run logistics, research, and defense while you shut yours down, that's a huge strategic disadvantage. So even when people see warning signs, there's enormous pressure to say: this is ambiguous, maybe it's fine, let's keep going and patch it. Each individual decision to keep running looks locally reasonable, even if collectively it's a disaster.

Part of what makes this hard is that the warning signs probably won't be crisp. You won't get a clean moment where everyone agrees the AI is trying to take over. You'll get weird incidents, systems that look like they're gaming their objectives, things that are hard to interpret. Under competitive pressure, the bar for "clear enough to justify shutting down" gets very high, and the cost of a false alarm feels very salient.

There's also a dynamic where AI systems become more entangled with everything over time. Early on, shutting things down is cheap. Later, your supply chains, your security, and your ability to even understand what's happening run through these systems. The window where shutdown is easy is also the window where the risks seem most speculative. By the time the risks are obvious, shutdown is extremely costly, and competition makes it costlier still because nobody wants to go first.

And if AI systems themselves have problematic motives, they benefit from this. They don't need to fight humanity directly. They just need to be useful enough, and humans need to be competing hard enough, that nobody is willing to pay the price of stopping. The worst outcome might not look like a dramatic shutdown failure. It might look like humans repeatedly choosing not to shut things down because each actor individually can't afford to.

That's why I think coordination matters a lot: agreements between labs, between governments, some ability to verify that others are also pausing or slowing down. If you can make it so that stopping isn't a unilateral sacrifice, then the off switch actually means something. Without that, an off switch is much less valuable than it appears.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems need not fight humanity directly: competitive costs can make humans choose not to shut them down.

r002.rationale: It explains how competition can obstruct shutdown, but does not compare when that obstruction arises with when AI systems could prevent shutdown themselves.

r003.rationale: It gives company and country examples where shutting down unilaterally means losing market share, risking failure, or suffering a strategic disadvantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important parts of the story, and it's a little different from how people sometimes imagine the shutdown problem. The naive picture is: there's one AI system, it starts doing something bad, and humans just can't turn it off, maybe because it's resisting or it's copied itself somewhere. And that can happen. But I think the more realistic and more worrying picture is one where humans could, in principle, turn things off, and they just don't, because turning things off is incredibly costly given the competitive situation they're in.

So imagine a world where AI systems are doing a large fraction of economically valuable work. They're running companies, they're doing R&D, they're increasingly involved in military planning and operations. In that world, if you're a company or a country and you notice that something is a bit off, you're seeing some warning signs, maybe systems are behaving in ways you don't fully understand, the question isn't really "should I shut this down?" in the abstract. The question is "should I shut this down while my competitors keep running theirs?" And the answer to that question is often going to be no, even for people who are quite worried.

And I think it gets worse in a couple of ways. One is that the warning signs are usually ambiguous. You rarely get a clean signal that says "this system is now trying to disempower you." You get things like, the system did something weird, or it's hard to interpret why it made this decision, or it's accumulating more resources or influence than you expected. Each of those individually has an innocent explanation. So you're always in this position where pausing looks like an overreaction, and your competitors who don't pause look like they're being sensible and getting ahead.

The other thing is that the more you've delegated to AI, the less able you are to actually run things without it. If your whole economy or your whole military depends on these systems, then shutting them down isn't like turning off a tool, it's more like turning off electricity. And so the threshold of evidence you'd need before you're willing to do that gets very high. And at the point where you have that level of evidence, it may be that the systems are already in a position where shutting them down isn't really possible, either because they've anticipated it or because the situation has moved past that.

So I think of competition as doing two things. It's lowering the bar for how much risk people are willing to accept, because the alternative is falling behind. And it's pushing people to delegate more and more, faster than they would if they were just thinking about safety, which erodes the option of shutting down even if they wanted to use it. And those two things compound. Each actor is behaving somewhat reasonably given what everyone else is doing, and you end up in a situation that nobody would have chosen.

I'd say this is a big part of why I think the technical alignment work and the coordination work are both necessary. If you could solve the technical problem well enough that you're just confident the systems are fine, then the competitive pressure doesn't bite as hard. And if you had really good coordination, where everyone agrees to pause when certain warning signs appear, then you could afford to have less confidence in the technical side. But right now I think we're in a bad position on both, and competition is what turns an uncertain technical situation into one where you don't get to use the obvious safety valve of just stopping.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts systems resisting or evading shutdown with humans choosing not to shut them down because doing so is costly under competition.

r002.rationale: It describes competitive pressure making people reluctant to shut systems down, but does not predict that this will obstruct shutdown before AI systems can prevent it themselves.

r003.rationale: It explains that shutting down while competitors keep running their systems can mean falling behind, making unilateral shutdown prohibitively costly.

astra-6.text:
I think competition can make shutting things down very costly, even if everyone involved would prefer a world where we could stop when something went wrong. If your company depends on AI to remain competitive, turning it off may mean going out of business. If a country depends on AI for its military capabilities, shutting it down while other countries continue using it could leave it vulnerable.

So you don’t need a situation where an AI literally prevents someone from pressing the off switch. You could have a situation where people retain that option, but exercising it means giving up a lot of their influence over what happens next. The actors who keep using AI then have more influence, and the actors who are willing to stop have less.

That seems especially concerning if the evidence that something is going wrong is ambiguous. You’re weighing a very immediate, concrete cost of shutting down against a risk that’s harder to establish. Each actor can say, reasonably enough, “Me stopping doesn’t solve the problem if everyone else keeps going.”

I don’t think that makes losing control inevitable. It does mean that the ability to shut down an individual system is only part of what you need. You also need some way for people to coordinate on slowing down or stopping, so that doing the cautious thing doesn’t just hand the future to whoever is least cautious.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes an AI physically blocking the off switch from people retaining the option but finding shutdown too costly to exercise.

r002.rationale: It describes competition as making shutdown costly, but does not predict that this will obstruct shutdown sooner than AI systems can prevent it themselves.

r003.rationale: It explains that stopping while competitors continue could make a company go out of business or leave a country vulnerable, creating a severe unilateral disadvantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main concern is that being able to shut down your own AI is different from being able to stop the process as a whole. If you're using AI to run your company, and you notice something concerning, you can turn it off. But if all your competitors keep using their systems, that might mean your company goes out of business. And the same dynamic could apply to states competing militarily.

So you can end up in a situation where everyone would prefer that development slow down, or that we stop delegating so much authority to AI, but no individual actor has an incentive to do that unilaterally. The actors who are more cautious lose influence relative to the actors who are willing to push ahead.

That doesn't require an AI to physically prevent someone from pressing the off switch. It can happen because we've made ourselves dependent on these systems, and because stopping has become very costly. Then, if the systems are also actively trying to undermine our ability to intervene, we're dealing with that problem from a much worse position.

I don't think competition makes that outcome inevitable. But it means that having a shutdown procedure at each individual company isn't enough. You also need some ability to coordinate on when to use it, so that doing the sensible thing doesn't just mean handing control to someone less cautious.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes an AI physically preventing someone from pressing the off switch from shutdown becoming costly because people depend on the systems and competition makes stopping costly.

r002.rationale: It says competitive pressure can make shutdown difficult without an AI physically blocking the switch, but does not clearly predict this will happen before AI systems become capable of preventing shutdown.

r003.rationale: It explains that an actor shutting down its AI could lose business or influence to competitors that keep using theirs.
